name: Arkansas
summary_text: Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Screening carries an outing risk independent of Arkansas law. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Several governments responded: in April 2025 CNN reported advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens.  Facilities restrictions apply across a widening band of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans covering trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Arkansas enacted Act 619 on 11 April 2023, becoming the fourth state to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender; the Movement Advancement Project's February 2026 citations record the measure as HB 1156, a 2023 K-12 facility ban amended and extended in 2025. Enforcement elsewhere has produced arrest: in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.  A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Arkansas in its "Worst Policies In Effect" group alongside Alabama, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Ohio, Oklahoma, North Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming, one tier below the four states graded "Do Not Travel": Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. Idaho reached that grade after a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years, partially court-blocked but in force where no gender-neutral option exists; Kansas is graded over a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime. The assessment records the 2026 legislative season as continuing to degrade trans rights while federal policy drives nationwide trends.  Federal custody and federal enforcement present documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.  Care access is constrained for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

name: Colorado
summary_text: Colorado stands within the United States federal framework, which sets the baseline a trans visitor carries into the state: Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, the State Department no longer issues the X marker and processes new passports only as M or F, the Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and TSA screening procedures can require secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that disclose a traveller's trans status. Visa discretion over transgender athletes applying to compete in women's sports, flagged with an internal marking and treated in some cases as grounds for a permanent ban, applies at any port of entry including Denver.  State law in Colorado runs against that current. The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act expressly covers gender identity and gender expression across employment, housing and public accommodations, and the legislature expanded that coverage again in 2025. Public-accommodation coverage is the provision a visitor would rely on directly, in hotels, restaurants, shops and venues.  The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on 18 May 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law by suspending gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to enjoin the hospital into resuming puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing the same treatment for cisgender children while halting it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity.' Two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.  Care access still narrows on federal funding. Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage of hormone therapy, puberty blockers and related gender-affirming care for transgender youth from 13 October 2026, because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under 18 and under 19 through the CHP+ child programme. The state Medicaid agency says resuming coverage 'will require legislative action.' Patients already taking hormones retain coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected. A visitor needing continuing care should therefore expect the federal constraint to govern here rather than the state's protective posture.  A July 2026 national risk assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people, alongside California, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey, and counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage.  That posture faces a direct political test. Colorado voters decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender children from gendered sports not aligned with biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after elections officials certified signatures on the measures in March 2026. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and, if passed, would write restrictions on transgender minors into state law.  Incarceration risk in Colorado is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care; a court-approved 2024 consent decree in Denver District Court (Raven v. Polis) required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement, and relief has been won through court order rather than a baseline housing rule.

sources.title: Romer v. Evans - U.S. Supreme Court (1996)
sources.documents: Struck down Colorado Initiative 2 (1992 constitutional amendment) that prohibited protected status for homosexual, lesbian or bisexual orientation; holds amendment was motivated by animus and violated Equal Protection Clause of Fourteenth Amendment.
sources.detail: No URL visible in text. Cited as: 1994 Colorado Supreme Court found amendment unconstitutional; 1996 U.S. Supreme Court held in Romer v. Evans amendment 'allows discrimination against homosexuals and prevents the state from protecting them'.

sources.title: McDaniel-Miccio v. Hickenlooper + marriage equality orders (2014)
sources.documents: State-court challenge to Colorado marriage definition arguing civil unions created second-class citizenship; led to Oct 6-7, 2014 dismissal of appeal/lift of stay after 10th Circuit Oklahoma/Utah precedents, Colorado Supreme Court lifted barriers, AG John Suthers ordered clerks to issue licenses; plus Jan 2021 Colorado Supreme Court retroactive recognition of pre-2014 common-law same-sex marriages.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Cited as: Filed Feb 19, 2014 by nine same-sex couples; defendants Gov. Hickenlooper and Denver City Clerk; AG John Suthers.
